The main point of the game seems to be fending off the endless attacks of enemy aircraft.  You can only stay underwater so long.  Then you will have to fight them off using your guns.  Realistic? The most obvious is a sick graphics error that shows your command crew still on the bridge of the conning tower even after dive dive diving.  When in external view, you can see them search for enemy shipping with their binos while under the waves.  Maybe they will find the ships I sunk while I was in SH3.

review_text:
I can't really say this is my kind of game. I loved the tactics of R6 Siege and the R6 Vegas games and this seems like a combination of the two having the first person controls of Siege and the squad mechanics of Vegas, I think it's more tactical than the both of them as you can control multiple squads at once and there's multiple map objectives at a time, if you're not careful you can get one of your squad members killed or worse yourself. You die instantly in this game and if you do manage to survive you will remain injured until what I can only assume you either get healed by a medic or you just bleed out. I can't say for sure because I died before I could figure it out and this game is very old school in the way that it doesn't explain much. There is a tutorial but I skipped it, sound design was great, really captures that empty feeling of being in a jungle, and visually I loved the old school graphics, and the in game menus and minimap had this really old charm to them.

Downsides: The game wouldn't launch for me at first but after a few minutes of reading someone who had a similar issue as me related to AMD all I had to do was add a few characters of text to one of the game files to get it to launch, so not a big deal it didn't take me long to figure it out. Rebinding keys was a bit of a hassle to figure out at first since there's a lot of unnecessary ones like zoom in and out are two separate things, crouch and stand are separate, numbers are bound to a whole bunch of separate chat things whatever that's for. Honestly this game just isn't casual friendly and that isn't a bad thing as I'm sure it has it's audience. If you like more tactical based slow paced games or hell maybe even rts this game might be for you, but if you like modern shooters and want to pick up a game and just play it I wouldn't recommend...

But hell I got this game for $1.30CAD in a sale, I can't complain! I got my dollars worth of entertainment

Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy is a point-and-click adventure that answers the question:

> “What if we gave you Sherlock’s brain… but *none* of his patience?”

You’re invited to investigate a mysteriously abandoned mansion museum.
In practice, you will:

* Click on 3 pixels per second
* Solve 19th-century OSHA violations
* Develop a deep hatred of sarcophagi

---

### Pros:

* Peak early-2000s adventure energy: static pre-rendered rooms, weird camera angles, and puzzles designed by someone who’s never heard the phrase “too obscure.”
* Sherlock occasionally says something smug like, “Elementary,” after you solve a puzzle you brute-forced by randomly combining items for 10 minutes.
* Inventory full of extremely specific trash: broken rods, mysterious keys, clock hands, half a cog, some rope, one brick, emotional damage.
* Every room feels like an escape room built by a museum curator who *really* didn’t want visitors.

---

### Cons:

* Difficulty curve:

the gunplay in this game is surprisingly fluid and engaging, with a short time to kill every interaction comes down to spilt second reactions. the labyrinthian maps, the short respawn time, and constant hail of grenades simulates the experience of being a nameless soldier who exists only to take as many lives as possible before losing his own. the sprinting, while creative and should be further explored in the future, is unintuitive. it uses a standard sprint meter, depleting when used, recharging when walking or standing (faster through the latter method), however the depletion of the meter is not linear, but incremental, causing the bar to lower in short bursts that play at a consistent rate. this means that in theory you can memorize this timing in order to optimize your meter, but with the chaos the rounds already bring this idea is washed away in the players mind. 

8/10

Legitimately one of my favorite games ever. Brilliant brilliant brilliant. It's hard without being too monotonous or cheap (though there are some gotchas lol). The onboarding process with the controls is a little unforgiving, but once you learn it, it's actually incredibly precise. There is some very slight tedium at times because you can only call Mudokons one at a time in this, but oh well. It's still great.

I played the remake before I played this version, and the remake isn't *bad*, but they drop some of the difficulty, which I quite like, and imo the controls mostly feel worse. The remake also removes some of the aesthetic sauce by making everything feel less weighty and brightening everything. If you can get it working, play this instead, and if it's too hard for your liking (nothing wrong with that fyi), try New & Tasty.

It is so bleak in its circumstances, and yet, without being hokey and instead perfectly sincere in its conviction, decides that the most radical action is community, hope, and love. I love that.

Having played multiple iterations of Oddworld games over several years, I can say with confidence that Oddworld has genuinely improved my life, the best of compliments that I can give. The original devs should be proud. Abe's Oddysee is amazing. Now time to play Abe's Exoddus!

review_text:
Bionic Commando (2009) is pretty funny, even though it feels like it takes itself too seriously. It’s unclear if that was intentional or not, but either way it ends up being hilarious. There are a ton of F-bombs and a lot of different tropes that make it kind of entertaining in a weird way.

It’s also funny how a lot of the NPCs are on a first-name basis with the protagonist. They say “I’m going to F*** You up Spencer” all the time, like they have a personal gripe with him, and something about that just lands.

The game runs pretty well overall, but it does feel kind of janky, especially with the grappling. There are moments where the character gets stuck on a wall trying to jump off, and won’t unlatch unless the game is paused. Not sure if that’s user error or the game, but it happens more than once.

Combat actually feels really good at times. Headshots make that clean “ding” sound that’s super satisfying, and the sniper getting one-shot kills just feels great every time. It’s also super cool being able to grab soldiers with the bionic arm and toss them off cliffs.

The ‘90s action movie ridiculousness really stands out. The pacing is well done, it doesn’t take long to complete, and it never overstays its welcome. There’s also that old-school vibe where it feels like every main bad guy is European.

The character model from the tutorial would have been a better choice, more like the older Spencer from Bionic Commando Rearmed with the red hair and cool sunglasses. That version looks way better than the one with dreads in this game.

Originally picked up alongside Bionic Commando Rearmed for just $3.51 total for both games. 

I got the platinum trophy on PS3 back in 2010, and coming back for that nostalgic hit does not disappoint. The PC version looks phenomenal after all these years. It’s surprising there aren’t Steam achievements in this one.

A remake would actually be really interesting, especially if it leaned into a more fluid swinging style like the Insomniac Spider-Man games. Capcom feels like a perfect fit for that kind of gameplay, and it would be great to see them explore that concept. 

Overall, it’s a mix of janky gameplay, ‘90s action tropes, and unintentionally funny moments, but that kind of makes it memorable.

Bejeweled 2 Deluxe
★☆★☆★☆★☆★☆★

Summary - A complete expansion on the original with a cool cosmic theme and a soundtrack that puts you in a flow state. If you are looking for a game to calm the mind, I recommend losing yourself in this cosmic journey.

__The Gameplay (★★★★☆) __ 
It's a match 3 puzzle game, so the premise is very simple and easy to understand. This game has plenty of modes to choose and from what I can remember as a kid, you will need to play A LOT of bejeweled to unlock everything there is be experienced in this game. The bonus modes are mainly abridged version of the mode they replace and are there mainly to reward your dedication (I love Hyper mode). Like most early Popcap classics, there are a handful of easter eggs to spice up your planetary expedition.

__The Visuals & OST (★★★★☆)__ 
Obviously cleaner than the last. The theme here is this alien feel. Mix that in with bejewels usual soundtrack that has you feeling transcendence and it all comes together near perfectly. I say near, because the music kind of blends a little tooooo well. Like it all feels the same.  

__Over all Rating (8/10)__ 
This game is a good grab if it's on sale and whether you are new to the series or experienced in the past, it is definitely worth launching into this vibrant classic.

★☆★☆★☆★☆★☆
Dynomite! Deluxe
★☆★☆★☆★☆★☆

Summary - A fun puzzle pop game that takes you on a ride through the age of the dinosaurs. Whether it the classic endless mode or the fun puzzle modes on the side, this game was a childhood staple, and a fun game to play in the background while conversing in a VC. For it's size, I'd say get it on sale.

__The Gameplay (★★★⯪☆) __ 
It keeps itself simple. It's one of those puzzle games that feel good to master, whether it be going speedy for endless or taking your time and planning out on puzzle mode. Your performance can choose how difficult you want it to be, with Whirly attempting to bring more color and complexity to the stage as you play. It takes some time to get used to, especially if you want to grind for the top and beat Tank on the leaderboard. Fossil mode is easily the most fun in my opinion. Putting a more strategic spin on the gameplay than it had before.

__The Visuals & Sound (★★★★☆)__ 
It's all a vibe. You got those chill flute tracks playing while you trick shot and explode eggs left and right, that stone age theme goes well with the jungle setting in the background, it's comfy for it's small resolution.

__Over all Rating (7/10)__
A small game and the price fits for the experience you'll have. It's a classic and like how each combo goes through time periods, it's pretty timeless.

Well, for some reason, I bought this game. Probably because I thought to myself "Wow, a Bethesda game I've never played! Surely this might be some forgotten gem of high quality, right?"

Nope. Wrong. Really should've skipped this one.

Basically, generic fantasy land is beset by troublesome orcs and demons and dragons. You play as bald warrior or big tit elf on a quest to save the land from.....ah, hell, who am I kidding? Even watching the cutscenes I tuned out of the plot a few hours in. It really doesn't matter. You're basically playing a mid version of a cross between Gears of War and Diablo.

Let me get the positives out of the way....The voice acting is superb. Laura Bailey, Graham McTavish, and Lucy Lawless all do a phenomenal job with a very forgettable script, but their characters are somewhat believable, if not memorable in the slightest. The combat is repetitive, but it' does the job well.

And that's about as much as I can say positive about this game. It is just so forgettable. It feels unpolished, buggy, and a chore to finish. I only played it because I wanted something kinda big and dumb after playing some very story driven RPGs.

The graphics are very ugly, even at max settings. Textures look choppy and dull and brown. It seems like all the attention to detail went into making the female characters have gigantic tits and look like a Suicide Girls cosplay mixed with Xena the Warrior Princess. Half the time when Lucy Lawless was talking, I was thinking "MAN LOOK AT THOSE BAZOOGAS!"

Also, there are spells in the game, but really, the only one that's useful is Caddoc's dash attack that breaks shields. So I just ended up spamming the hell out of that and basically got the job done.

There are side quests, but I didnt do any of them. I did one early one and it was a slog, so I just assumed the side quests were slogs as well that ruin the pacing.

Also, what is the point of gold in this game? You cant buy anything at a store. Like, seriously, what is the point of this?

I find it hard to believe that these are the same devs that made the excellent Wasteland sequels and Torment: Tides of Numenera, Those games have incredible stories, great gameplay, fascinating writing, etc etc etc. I guess you gotta make a few stinkers before you move on to the good stuff>

Look, it's not the worst game ever made. For 5 bucks, you really could do a lot worse. But it sure as shit ain't great, memorable, or even halfway decent. It's a game. It works. If you want something dumb and fun, it can be enjoyable. Just sink about 8-9 hours and move in. I certainly did.

★☆★☆★☆★☆★☆★☆★
Heavy Weapon Deluxe
★☆★☆★☆★☆★☆★☆★

Summary - A shoot'em up that will have you feeling that American pride. The skies are showered with bombs and communist invaders and it's up to you to counter and bring freedom to the military continent. Ride Atomic Tank, you are our only hope. I realize just how crazy it feels to have this game come from PopCap of all teams.

__The Gameplay (★★★☆☆) __ 
Every level has a select set of waves the game randomly chooses, and if you can mark them down they are fun to practice and improve in. The Atomic Tank is allowed one upgrade per level (you have to upgrade before proceeding), allowing you to customize just what you desire for all your commie killing needs (I can't believe those words would ever come out of my head). There's a ton of enemy variety and the waves can get pretty difficult to react in. If you can't get enough levels and upgrades, there is a survival mode that goes on forever to test your true skill as an Ultimate Tanker. The major problem I see people talking about is the fact you can only control with mouse. Your distance between you and the cursor affects speed, strength, and control. I personally find it satisfying to get the hang of.

__The Atmosphere (★★★★☆) __ 
I love how everything is themed after military weaponry and tanks. The levels all being quite unique (one is just Russia lmao). I enjoyed whenever you used a nuke, it would affect some of the features in the background. Like dang, I just killed a ton of innocent citizens. later levels can get quite chaotic with bombs showering the skies like a dense pattern in a bullet hell, luckily you have the power to counter with your own storm of bullets and missiles.

review_text:
I remember when Bionic Commando Rearmed first came out on the PlayStation 3. I bought it right away and absolutely loved the music, the gameplay, and just the overall feel of it. Later, when I switched to PC, I was so excited to see it was available there too. It was the same with the other Bionic Commando game—the one with the dreads. I bought both of them back when they originally released on PS3.

Back then, I remember Rearmed being incredibly difficult, and I never managed to beat it. Coming back to it now reminded me why I liked it so much. The controls feel really tight, and the swinging mechanic is still one of the coolest movement systems in any platformer.

This was actually the first game I played on my ROG Ally X. Ironically, I could never get it working properly on my desktop PC, even after trying a bunch of tutorials online. The handheld had no issues, so I ended up playing the entire game there.

One thing I really like is that this isn’t a Metroidvania. You simply pick a level, beat it, and move on. Every stage feels like its own platforming puzzle, and the bosses are puzzles too. It’s not just about having fast reflexes—you have to figure out each boss’s mechanics before you can beat them, which makes every fight feel rewarding.

There are around 19 levels. Some are full stages while others are shorter transition areas, but I actually like that structure because I can jump into a level, focus on beating it, and call it a day instead of wandering through one giant interconnected map. Defeating bosses also rewards you with new weapons and upgrades, like bazookas, pistol upgrades, machine guns, and character enhancements, so it always feels like you’re making progress.

Now for the part where I have a love-hate relationship with the game: that final level. It honestly felt as long as, if not longer than, all the previous stages. It reminded me of the old Gauntlet games where you have a limited number of lives and just keep inching a little farther every attempt. I had to memorize every section. The Albatross stage in particular really was the albatross around my neck—I genuinely thought I wasn’t going to beat the game because of it.

Even after getting through all those sections, you only have so many lives left for the final boss. Eventually I got consistent enough to reach the boss with five lives almost every run, but then I had to learn the boss itself, which is also extremely difficult. The frustrating part is that it takes so long to get back to the fight that practicing the boss is a challenge in itself.

When I finally beat it, though, it felt amazing. It wasn’t one of those “I’m just glad it’s over and never want to play it again” moments. It was the kind of victory that feels earned. I’m pretty sure if I went back now I’d beat that final level much faster because it’s one of those games where persistence and learning the patterns eventually pays off.

I also played the game on the hardest difficulty available for a brand-new save file. I know there’s an even harder difficulty that unlocks afterward, but this was the toughest setting you can choose from the start, and it felt like the perfect challenge.

Overall, I loved Bionic Commando Rearmed. The soundtrack is fantastic, the controls are incredibly tight, the swinging mechanic is still one of the most satisfying movement systems around, and I really enjoyed the level-by-level structure instead of another Metroidvania. It’s a challenging game, but one that always feels fair once you learn it.

It’s also a shame that Bionic Commando Rearmed 2 isn’t available on Steam. I’ve heard it’s not nearly as good, but I’d still like the chance to play it because this game reminded me why I liked the series so much in the first place.

This is genuinely the only multiplayer game that doesn't make me mad while I play. I never even get the urge to strangle my opponents. Despite coming out in 1999, it's still incredibly fun to play, and the visuals have aged surprisingly well they don’t look jarring at all. 

The core gameplay is exactly what an arena shooter should be. Every weapon in your arsenal has a specific, highly tactical purpose. The movement is really smooth; you can double your speed by strafe jumping, and rocket jumping is a staple Quake mechanic that needs no introduction. 

The combat loop is perfectly balanced: you can use the Plasma Gun for slight wall-climbing tricks or long range harassment, pick off low-health targets with the Machine Gun, or shred them up close with the Shotgun. The Railgun is your long-range damage dealer a guaranteed two-tap on unarmored targets while the Rocket Launcher is really great for map control and prefiring corners. I haven't actually beaten Heretic OR the original HeXen.
That being said, from what little I've played of HeXen 1, HeXen II is MILES better! The levels and progression from area to area can be a bit obtuse, but it beats the Hell out of needing to find a dozen switches just to open a door. And I would argue that unique items relating to each unique area being the driving force of unlocking secrets to get to the next stage is far more interesting anyway.

The combat takes some getting used to with certain weapons and/or characters, ESPESCIALLY if you insist on playing without a crosshair (which I do 🙃), but just choose a difficulty that feels fair in order to get used to the combat. And then once you're ready, move up a difficulty level on your next playthrough!

It still has some jank, you'll need some community patches and a source port to get the best experience, and there WILL BE parts that make you go "What the HELL am I supposed to do?!" but honestly, it's par for the course when it comes to these early action adventure games.

It's not DOOM, it's not Heretic 2, and it's not Unreal, but it's a Raven game, and that's enough for me. 👌

It’s alright, not as jagged or weird as quake 1 which makes it way less interesting as a piece of video game history imo. A lot of people say that the visuals in this game are really bland and I have to agree. Lots of browns and greys. Not that quake 1 was bursting with saturated colors or anything, but the gothic and medieval horror vibe of quake 1 was more interesting from a tonal perspective than the straightforward sci-fi feel of this game. That first game was so inscrutable and moody and it felt like the dark color palette was a big part of that. A sci-fi setting could’ve benefited from a little bit more color and detail, but it feels like they just did the visuals of quake 1 again without understanding why the dingy aesthetic of that game fit so well. 

It’s worth noting that Trent Reznor, who refused to come back to the series to do the ost for quake 2 as he did for the original, voiced a lot of these criticisms too. He said quake 2 had no atmosphere. I don’t know if I fully agree with that, but put up against the first game it’s easy to see where he’s coming from. Maybe he didn’t feel like the game was sufficiently dissonant enough for his tastes. Quake 1’s single player is nothing if not atonal and weird. It’s a game with hastily thrown together elements from completely contrasting vibes, level designers who couldn’t agree on anything, and with almost no attempt to make it cohere at all. It is something that you would never see today. No serious or experienced game designer in 2026 would even think to make something like Quake 1. Quake 2, unlike basically any other game, suffers by sticking to a more coherent vision. 

I wish I could post a review without having to give a thumbs up or thumbs down bc this is one of those cases where you’ll probably enjoy it if you just love boomer shooters I guess. I’m giving it a thumbs up just because thumbs down seems a little mean

review_text:
Call of Juarez is a great Western Shooter released in 2007 with a impressive shared two protagonist storyline that takes you on a journey with both of them, with two different themes, one with overcoming fear and developing worth for oneself without letting others tell you who you are; and the other theme of Redemption. Billy and Ray are well written characters with their conflicts, Ray especially at the beginning will feel like self righteous priest who praises the word of God but as the story progresses we find out why he even became a priest and what price he paid for changing his way, and the voice acting in that revelation is especially exceptionally good. Voice acting of both the protagonist is really good but Ray's voice actor really delivers a wonderful performance. I also really like Episodic way of storytelling which I also very much enjoyed in COJ: Gunslinger but what I also like is how in this game the loading screens for Episodes also serve to tell the story of the protagonist through their monologue and like I said before the voice acting in those monologues is really good, these monologues serve the purpose of both giving background for the characters and also progress the story in some way.

As far as the Graphics are concerned, for the time it was released it looks really good, especially the environment which really has great overall Wild West vibe to it. The gameplay is overall preset decent, considering the time it was released in, I think the gunfights are pretty decent, they are not RDR or Gunslinger level, because those came much later, but for its time, the gameplay is pretty fine. Also I liked how in some missions, despite not being an open world, it gives you a lot of space to explore, almost acting like semi world, your freedom to explore is limited but it is there, which I think is good.

There are some flaws though, like with Whips/lasso having a very tight hit box and the option to swing using a lasso by using a tree branch only appears at a specific angle and so more often than not you would have to struggle to find the right angle to use the Lasso and it becomes frustrating sometimes especially if you have pursuers in a mission. Also, some Episodes (5 and 9) may have some bugs or may crash, like in Episode 5 specifically, I was facing a crash near the end of that mission, after some troubleshooting I fixed it with Downgrading to DirectX9 version of the game (I was playing on DirectX 10 version before) only for that specific segment and something similar happened at the start of Episode 9 I believe where the game would crash at the beginning which again I fixed by downgrading for that specific segment and then switching back to DirectX 10 version. Apart from this, some missions may seem drawn out but that isn't necessarily a bad thing, because it also adds to the tension and atmosphere but some people may find it annoying and tedious.

Overall, its a great game with impressive story and voice acting, a bit dated in some areas, but barring a few issues here and there, it is an amazing 2000s western shooter that is worth playing.

Finally, I've got my closure with franchise as an old fan since my very childhood (my father was a big fan, we  had 1, 2, Tactics and 3 on CDs back in 2000s, played Fallout 4 during the first months of its release (honestly, we pirated it, but tss). Not so long ago I finally finished FNV.

Do I like the gameplay? Hell yeah, shooting feels good, loot is awesome, variability, mechanics (especially on Hardcore mode). 

Long story short - highly recommend. Play it - and we'll find out about Mojave making you wish for a nuclear winter.

Saints Row 2 isn't just a game. It's a lifestyle.

review_text:
Abe's Oddysee is still a classic, but running it on a modern PC takes a bit of setup. Out of the box, my CPU fans blew like crazy and hit 75C because the 1997 engine runs an uncapped single-core loop that pushes one CPU core at full boost voltage, even on the main menu.

I spent a long time testing standard fixes like setting a global or program specific max frame rate in GPU software, or changing CPU affinity in Task Manager and researched other solutions but didn't bother trying riskier things with the registry, BIOS and so on. None of what I tried worked because they don't stop the internal code loop from maxing out that single core.

Here is what actually fixed everything for me:

1. Finding & Adding the Executable
Auto-scans in GPU software won't detect this game. You have to manually add AbeWin.exe to your NVIDIA graphics program settings as well as Windows Graphics Settings to force your dedicated GPU (if you have a CPU with integrated graphics) and apply other custom profile options. (However frame limiters won't work like I said earlier.)

2. Visual & Scaling Fixes
Right-click AbeWin.exe > Properties > Compatibility tab:

Check Disable fullscreen optimizations.

Click Change high DPI settings, check Override high DPI scaling behavior, and set it to Application.

In your GPU control panel or App, make sure the scaling device is your GPU, Override the Scaling Mode Set by Games and Programs is checked and lastly enable GPU Integer Scaling as the mode. On a 1440p monitor, this gives you a sharp 1920x1440 centered picture with clean black sidebars instead of a blurry stretched image that aspect ratio gives. For other resolutions, you'll have to research that because integer scaling needs to divide evenly to work best, but on a 2560x1440p display panel the math works out for integer scaling with this game; you can switch back to Aspect Ratio whenever for other games. 

3. Fixing the CPU Heat & Fan Noise
Go to Windows Control Panel > Hardware and Sound > Power Options > Create a Power Plan (left side of the window) > create a custom plan name at the bottom (I named mine "Old Games")  and save it with default options > Change Plan Settings > Change Advanced Power Settings > Processor Power Management > set Maximum Processor State to 95%. This turns off CPU Turbo Boost voltage spikes for any programs while the plan is on, dropping my CPU temps from 75C down to a completely silent 41C with zero performance loss. I made a desktop shortcut for Power Options to swap to this plan when playing old unoptimized games like this that lack normal support.

Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood is a prequel to the Original Call of Juarez released in 2006, this story follows the McCall brothers, Ray and Thomas, and their journey after the American Civil war but the one narrating is the third brother named, William, a good young man, trying to guide his brothers to the right path. After playing it thoroughly, I can confidently say this game has the best story in the entire series, even better than Gunslinger, even though I love Gunslinger but the multiple themes and the way characters development happens by the end of the story and even the Antagonist's character writing are definitely well done in this story. The loading screens are used to tell the story just like the first game but this time not in form of Monologue but instead by narration and the one narrating the events is William, and there are beautifully hand drawn frame by frame 2D animations which later became a staple of Call of Juarez: Gunslinger. 

Since it is a prequel to the first game, it reveals some unexpected things which later makes sense in the first game, which I also found very interesting. For instance a major character that just doesn't look like someone from the first game, is later revealed to be a major character in the first game all along.

As far as the Graphics are concerned, it looks really good for its time. In some chapters, it would make you completely forget that this game came out in 2009, some of scenery in the game is top notch and really looks beautiful and even the Character model and rest look pretty good for its time. The graphics can be a bit dated in some areas but it still looks better overall despite its age.

As for the Gameplay, you get to play as either Ray or Thomas for almost all chapters in the story. And both of their respective gameplay styles are really fun. Ray is fun for playing a Badass dual wielding Gunslinger who is strong and Sturdy, and Thomas is fun for playing a more agile and fast shooter, who can also use a rifle and a bow. Both of these playstyles are fun, whether you want to play it like a Badass Gunslinger (Ray) or an Agile Riflemen and Shooter (Thomas), both playstyles offer unique experiences. Also the Gunplay feels pretty good, especially with better and powerful weapons. Overall the gameplay is pretty fun and will grow on you as you play, it is not as polished as Gunslinger but still fun regardless.

The Cover system, this deserves a separate mention for how well designed it actually is. This game has possibly the best designed cover system I have ever seen in a video game. It works by crouching or just standing next to box or a pole and then you could move mouse slightly to shoot left or right, or you could just move it upwards and shoot without exposing yourself at all. I can't count just how many times cover system really helped in some tight situations in the game because it is well designed.

They have also improved up the lasso mechanic from the previous game and made it much better in this one, where in the previous a specific angel as required to even use lasso which made it very frustrating to use, but in this you could just aim and latch onto the thing and just either go up or down or just swing, which is an improvement over the previous title. Also the Dueling system in this one is fun too once you get the hang of it much like Duels in COJ: Gunslinger, it isn't as difficult as Gunslinger's Duel nor as convoluted as the first Call of Juarez's Duel system.

I also like the Free roam aspect as well. Even though this game is not open world, some chapters allow players to restock, make cash by doing some jobs or just free roam in the open world, so it is sort of semi-open world in that sense. Really enjoyed the bounty missions or taking down gangs in free roam, so those were fun too.

There are some flaws as well. Well for starters, the game doesn't have a New Game plus, despite the fact that the game has golden weapons (super variety) and build variety and some character specific route/content in chapters, it would add more replay value if the game had New Game Plus. In some of the chapters, a weapon shop is just casually open for you to buy weapons from while you are up against an entire town and all of the doors the shut, except for this weapon shop / Weapon merchant which is just casually open for business outside a Mexican bandit leader hideout or a Ghost town, etc. It isn't available in every chapter, only in a few and I understand it is there for gameplay convenience but it is bit immersion breaking, however it is not a big issue as it rarely occurs in chapters, most of the time you would miss except in free roam. 

Overall, Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood is a great and one of the best Western shooter experience with the franchise's most impressive story and a memorable Antagonist, along with great themes, soundtrack, graphics that still somewhat hold today plus charming and impactful characters and storyline that really deliver a great western experience, which makes it worth playing.

This is my first review on Steam.  
First: cap the frames to 60 (or 45 for Deck) to avoid physics bugs.  I played vanilla on Deck with no issues.  As of writing this review I am 80%+ through the main story (about 4 missions left) and have done quite a bit of side content.

I have completed all major Far Cry games on console (multiple times), but this is the best.  It is very disturbingly existential in its gameplay systems.  The factions give you pointless and amoral missions that serve only to perpetuate the conflict.  The routine nature of having to fix your vehicles, clear checkpoints,  and murder people to get to your objective.  The constant need to replace weapons and obtain malaria meds due to weapon and bodily degradation.  People say the respawning checkpoints are annoying, but without them the world would be empty and devoid of challenge.  Further, the checkpoints add to the feeling of futility and that you don't meaningfully impact the state of the country.  There is very little narrative; most of the game's expression of futile, routine, and amoral murder and chaos is expressed through its gameplay systems.  Most Far Cry games are morally ambiguous, but there is no ambiguity here, just pure amorality.  However, this is not going to be to everyone's taste.  Some people will find it frustrating and boring, I guess.  I loved it.  It does mess with your head a bit, though as it is a much bleaker game than the ones that came after.

Finally, the visuals are beautiful.  The character models are a bit dated, but passable, and the environment and atmosphere are top notch.

**The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Edition — A Timeless Fantasy RPG**

**Rating: 9/10 — Overwhelmingly Recommended**

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is one of those RPGs that makes it incredibly easy to lose yourself in another world. Even years after its original release, there is something special about exploring Cyrodiil, discovering forgotten ruins, joining different factions, and creating your own adventure in a vast fantasy world.

**Story and Quests:**

The main storyline follows the invasion of Tamriel by the forces of Oblivion, with the player becoming involved in a desperate attempt to stop the destruction spreading across the land. While the main quest is memorable, one of the game's greatest strengths is its side content.

The Dark Brotherhood and Thieves Guild questlines are particularly entertaining, offering memorable characters, interesting missions, and stories that often surpass expectations. The game also provides plenty of opportunities to make your character feel like a genuine part of the world rather than simply someone following the main storyline.

**World Design and Exploration:**

Cyrodiil is a wonderful setting to explore. Its forests, cities, villages, caves, ancient ruins, and distant mountains create a world that feels adventurous and full of possibilities. Simply wandering away from the main quest can lead to unexpected encounters, hidden locations, and interesting discoveries.

The world encourages curiosity, and that sense of freedom remains one of the game's greatest achievements.

**Gameplay and Character Progression:**

Oblivion offers considerable freedom in how you develop your character. You can become a warrior, mage, assassin, thief, or a combination of several different playstyles. Magic, melee combat, archery, stealth, alchemy, and persuasion provide different ways to approach challenges.

However, the original leveling system can be frustrating. Enemies often scale alongside the player, and the difficulty can become unbalanced if your character's attributes and combat abilities do not develop effectively. The combat itself also feels dated compared with modern RPGs, particularly when fighting enemies for extended periods.

Despite these shortcomings, the freedom to experiment with different builds remains enjoyable.

**Atmosphere, Music, and Visuals:**

The soundtrack is one of the game's strongest features. Its orchestral music perfectly complements the feeling of exploring a vast fantasy world, whether you are wandering through peaceful countryside or preparing to enter a dangerous dungeon.

Although the graphics and character animations have aged considerably, the art direction still has charm. The architecture, landscapes, fantasy creatures, and ancient ruins help create a recognizable identity that remains memorable.

**Characters and Immersion:**

The NPC schedules and interactions help make the world feel alive. Characters go about their daily routines, cities have their own personalities, and different factions offer opportunities to establish your place in society.

The voice acting can sometimes feel repetitive, and the facial animations are dated, but these imperfections contribute to the game's distinctive personality rather than completely undermining it.

**Expansions and Content:**

The Game of the Year Edition includes both major expansions: *Knights of the Nine* and *The Shivering Isles*.

*Knights of the Nine* offers a questline centered on recovering sacred relics and restoring a legendary order of knights. Meanwhile, *The Shivering Isles* introduces a bizarre new realm ruled by Sheogorath, the Daedric Prince of Madness. Its strange inhabitants, unusual quests, and distinctive atmosphere make it a particularly memorable addition.

Together, these expansions add substantial content to an already extensive RPG. Note that the standard Game of the Year Edition does not include every minor downloadable content pack found in the Deluxe Edition.

**Technical Performance and Age:**

As a game originally released in 2006, Oblivion has several technical limitations. The interface can feel clunky, animations are dated, and the original PC version may require some troubleshooting or community fixes depending on your system.

Nevertheless, these issues are generally outweighed by the sheer amount of freedom and content available. Players willing to accommodate an older RPG will find a great deal to enjoy.

**Final Verdict:**

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion remains an outstanding open-world RPG because of its freedom, memorable questlines, atmospheric soundtrack, expansive world, and opportunities for roleplaying. It is not without flaws, particularly in its leveling system, combat, and dated presentation, but its strengths have allowed it to remain enjoyable long after its original release.

The Game of the Year Edition is an excellent way to experience this classic, especially with both major expansions included.

If you enjoy fantasy RPGs, exploration, faction questlines, character customization, and the freedom to create your own adventures, Oblivion is absolutely worth playing.

**Final Rating: 9/10 — Highly Recommended. A classic RPG with an unforgettable world.**

**Call of Duty: World at War — One of the Greatest World War II Shooters Ever Made**

**Rating: 10/10 — A Must-Play Classic**

Call of Duty: World at War is one of the most memorable entries in the Call of Duty franchise. Developed by Treyarch, this 2008 first-person shooter delivers a brutal portrayal of World War II, combining intense combat, a dark atmosphere, an excellent soundtrack, and one of the most iconic bonus modes in gaming history: Nazi Zombies.

Even years after its release, World at War remains an outstanding example of how to create a memorable military shooter.

**Story and Campaign:**

One of the game's greatest strengths is its two-part campaign, which follows American Marines fighting against Imperial Japanese forces in the Pacific and Soviet soldiers battling Nazi Germany on the Eastern Front.

The American campaign emphasizes the brutality of jungle warfare, with ambushes, fortified positions, and relentless enemy resistance. The Soviet campaign takes a darker approach, following the Red Army's advance toward Berlin through some of the war's most devastating battles.

The characters, particularly Dimitri Petrenko and Viktor Reznov, help make the Soviet storyline especially memorable. The relationship between these characters adds emotional weight to the campaign, while the struggle to survive gives the battles a sense of desperation.

World at War does not attempt to present war as glamorous. Its disturbing imagery, violent encounters, and desperate situations emphasize the terrible human cost of the conflict.

**Gameplay and Combat:**

The gameplay follows the traditional Call of Duty formula, featuring linear missions, intense firefights, weapon variety, and explosive set pieces. The combat feels satisfying, and the different environments provide some welcome variation.

The Pacific missions introduce Japanese tactics such as ambushes and Banzai charges, while the Eastern Front features large-scale infantry battles and the destruction of German defensive positions.

The arsenal includes period-inspired weapons such as the M1 Garand, Thompson, PPSh-41, Mosin-Nagant, and MP40. Flamethrowers and other specialized weapons also add variety to certain encounters.

However, the grenade spam on higher difficulties can become extremely frustrating. Enemy AI can sometimes feel unfair, and friendly soldiers are not always as helpful as they should be. Despite these problems, the core shooting mechanics remain enjoyable.

**Historical Setting and Atmosphere:**

World at War excels at creating an intense World War II atmosphere. The battlefields, ruined buildings, jungle environments, military equipment, and sound design contribute to a convincing sense of chaos.

The game also gives attention to the Pacific theater, which was less frequently explored in mainstream military shooters than the European theater. Its portrayal of the fighting against Imperial Japanese forces gives the campaign a different character from games focused exclusively on the Western Front.

Although it takes creative liberties for dramatic purposes, the game successfully communicates the violence, exhaustion, and desperation associated with the conflict.

**Graphics and Visual Presentation:**

For a game released in 2008, World at War has impressive visual presentation. The environments are detailed enough to establish a strong sense of place, while the lighting, explosions, smoke, and destruction help create intense battle scenes.

The graphics are understandably dated today, but the art direction and cinematic presentation remain effective. The game still manages to deliver memorable moments without relying on modern graphical technology.

**Soundtrack and Sound Design:**

The audio is one of the game's strongest features. Weapon sounds, explosions, battlefield shouting, and environmental effects help make the combat feel chaotic and dangerous.

The soundtrack also deserves recognition for reinforcing the intensity of the campaign. Its music fits the game's darker tone, particularly during the Soviet missions, where the atmosphere becomes increasingly desperate.

Voice acting is another highlight, especially in the Soviet campaign. The dialogue between Reznov and Petrenko helps establish the emotional core of the story.

**Nazi Zombies — An Iconic Game Mode:**

Nazi Zombies is arguably one of World at War's greatest contributions to gaming. Originally unlocked after completing the campaign, this survival mode places players in increasingly difficult rounds of undead enemies.

Players must collect points, purchase weapons, repair barricades, unlock areas, and work together to survive for as long as possible. Every round becomes more dangerous, creating a satisfying mixture of tension, strategy, and cooperation.

The original Nacht der Untoten map is simple but incredibly effective, while later maps such as Verrückt, Shi No Numa, and Der Riese expand the experience with new mechanics, locations, and secrets.

Nazi Zombies helped establish a formula that would become a major part of the Call of Duty franchise. Its replayability, cooperative gameplay, and memorable atmosphere make it one of the game's most important features.

**Multiplayer and Cooperative Gameplay:**

The original multiplayer offers class-based combat, customizable loadouts, weapon progression, perks, and maps inspired by the game's World War II setting. Tank combat also adds an unusual element compared with many other entries in the series.

The cooperative campaign is another welcome feature, allowing friends to experience the story together rather than limiting cooperation to separate multiplayer modes.

However, the online experience deserves a qualification in a modern review. Because the game is nearly two decades old, its original multiplayer ecosystem is less convenient than that of newer titles. Players may encounter compatibility problems, limited populated lobbies, or other technical complications depending on how they access the game.

**Difficulty and Replayability:**

World at War can be brutally difficult, particularly on Veteran difficulty. Enemies are aggressive, grenades can become overwhelming, and surviving certain encounters requires patience and careful positioning.

Although this difficulty can sometimes feel unfair, it gives the campaign a memorable level of intensity. Completing difficult missions provides a genuine sense of accomplishment.

Nazi Zombies adds substantial replayability, while cooperative play, higher difficulty settings, and multiplayer provide additional reasons to return.

**Technical Performance and Weaknesses:**

Despite its strengths, World at War is not perfect. Its grenade-heavy encounters, occasionally unreliable friendly AI, dated animations, and repetitive firefights can become frustrating.

Modern PC players may also encounter legacy compatibility or online connectivity issues. The game was designed for much older systems, and some of its original online features are not as straightforward to use today.

These shortcomings are worth acknowledging, but they do little to diminish the quality of the campaign and Zombies mode.

**Final Verdict:**

Call of Duty: World at War remains an exceptional World War II shooter. Its two campaigns offer memorable combat and a darker atmosphere than many contemporary military games, while its soundtrack, characters, and level design help it stand out among other entries in the franchise.

Nazi Zombies alone gives the game considerable replay value, and its influence on later Call of Duty titles is difficult to overlook.

Although its difficulty balance, technical limitations, and aging multiplayer experience prevent it from being flawless, its strongest features have stood the test of time.

If you enjoy World War II history, military shooters, cooperative campaigns, and classic round-based survival games, Call of Duty: World at War is absolutely worth playing.

# **R.U.S.E.™ — A Brilliant World War II Strategy Experience**

**Rating: 9/10 — Highly Recommended**

R.U.S.E.™ is one of the most distinctive real-time strategy games set during World War II. It combines large-scale military operations, tactical deception, resource management, and strategic planning into an experience where victory depends on more than simply building the largest army.

**Story and Campaign:**

The campaign follows American officer Joe Sheridan through a series of World War II military operations. Players participate in battles across the European theater, completing objectives that require careful planning, effective leadership, and tactical adaptability. Although the story is not particularly character-driven, it provides an engaging framework for the strategic gameplay.

**Gameplay and Strategy:**

The gameplay revolves around building military infrastructure, producing units, managing resources, and commanding forces across expansive battlefields. Infantry, tanks, artillery, aircraft, and anti-tank units each serve different purposes, making combined-arms warfare essential.

Players must carefully balance offense and defense while protecting their infrastructure and exploiting weaknesses in enemy positions. Rushing into battle without proper preparation can quickly lead to defeat.

**Deception Mechanics:**

The game's defining feature is its deception system. Players can use misinformation, camouflage, reconnaissance, and fake offensives to manipulate enemy decisions.

A convincing decoy attack can draw enemy forces away from an important position, allowing your real offensive to succeed elsewhere. This creates a psychological dimension rarely explored so thoroughly in strategy games.

Success depends not only on understanding the battlefield but also on anticipating what your opponent believes is happening.

**Battlefield Design and Atmosphere:**

R.U.S.E. features expansive maps that encourage flanking maneuvers, defensive planning, and coordinated military operations. Its distinctive tabletop presentation makes battles resemble miniature military war rooms, reinforcing the feeling of commanding an entire army.

The combination of detailed terrain, moving formations, and large-scale engagements creates a memorable military atmosphere.

**Graphics and Sound Design:**

Although its graphics show their age, the game's visual presentation remains distinctive. Its zoom system allows players to switch between individual units and the wider battlefield, making it easier to appreciate the scale of operations.

The sounds of artillery, aircraft, engines, and gunfire complement the military atmosphere, while the soundtrack reinforces the tension of commanding forces during wartime.

**Multiplayer and Replayability:**

Multiplayer offers considerable strategic depth because human opponents can adapt their tactics and use deception unpredictably. Different maps, unit compositions, and approaches to warfare encourage experimentation and replayability.

However, the game's age means players should verify current multiplayer availability before purchasing specifically for online matches.

**Technical Performance and Weaknesses:**

R.U.S.E. has several limitations, including aging graphics, occasional repetitive encounters, and a learning curve that may frustrate newcomers. Its campaign is enjoyable but does not offer particularly deep character development.

Modern purchasing and online accessibility can also be challenging, depending on the platform and edition.

Nevertheless, these weaknesses do not diminish the originality of its strategic mechanics.

**Final Verdict:**

R.U.S.E.™ is an excellent strategy game that distinguishes itself through military deception, tactical planning, resource management, and large-scale World War II battles.

Its greatest strength is making intelligence and misinformation essential parts of warfare. Victory comes from understanding your opponent, concealing your intentions, and choosing the right moment to strike.

If you enjoy World War II history, military strategy, combined-arms warfare, and games that reward clever planning over mindless aggression, R.U.S.E.™ is highly recommended.

review_text:
I honestly didn't expect to get this invested in EVE Online. I downloaded it out of curiosity, thinking it would be another space MMO where you pick a ship, complete some missions, fight enemies and slowly upgrade your equipment. Well, I couldn't have been more wrong.

The first thing that stands out is just how much freedom this game gives you. There isn't really one correct way to play. You can become a miner, explorer, trader, industrialist, pirate or focus entirely on combat. You can spend hours building your economy, transporting goods between systems, searching for hidden locations or joining other players in large-scale fleet operations. And somehow, all these activities are connected to each other.

The player-driven economy is probably one of my favourite aspects. Almost everything has a purpose, and the market feels like an actual ecosystem rather than a shop with items randomly generated by developers. Players produce ships, gather resources, manufacture equipment and transport goods across the galaxy. Even something as simple as buying a new ship can involve a surprisingly complicated chain of player activities behind the scenes.

I also really like the atmosphere. Flying through different star systems, looking at distant planets, stations and massive ships gives you a strange feeling of being part of something much bigger than your own character. Sometimes I just find myself travelling somewhere with music playing in the background, checking the map and planning my next destination. It sounds boring on paper, but there is something relaxing about it.

Of course, EVE isn't perfect. The learning curve is absolutely brutal for newcomers. There are so many menus, statistics, mechanics and things to understand that it can feel like starting a new job rather than playing a game. The tutorials help, but they only introduce a fraction of what is actually available. You will probably spend quite a bit of time looking things up, watching guides and asking more experienced players for advice.

Another thing worth mentioning is that the game doesn't always respect your expectations. You can spend hours collecting resources or preparing for an expedition and lose everything because of one bad decision or an encounter with another player. Ships are not simply temporary equipment that magically returns after destruction. Losing something expensive genuinely hurts, especially when you know how much time it took to afford it. The community is another interesting part of the experience. You can meet incredibly helpful people willing to explain complicated mechanics, share knowledge and even help you get started. I guess that's part of the charm of a universe where other players are not just background characters.

I wouldn't recommend rushing through everything or trying to understand the entire game immediately. There is simply too much content, and constantly comparing your progress to experienced players is probably the fastest way to burn yourself out. Find an activity you enjoy, learn it properly and expand from there. Joining a decent corporation can also completely change your experience.

It's complicated, sometimes frustrating, occasionally incredibly slow, and definitely not for everyone. But if you enjoy space exploration, strategy, economics, social interaction and the freedom to create your own goals, there is a good chance you'll find something special here.

review_text:
STAR TREK ONLINE – A GREAT GAME STILL RUINED IN 2026 BY GREED AND AN INFLATED ECONOMY

Rating: 3/5 Stars

Star Trek Online has plenty going for it. The storylines, extensive selection of starships, customisation options and space combat make it an enjoyable experience, particularly for Star Trek fans. The developers deserve credit for keeping the game alive for over 16 years.

Unfortunately, much of that enjoyment is undermined by its ridiculously inflated player-driven Exchange.

The Exchange allows players to buy and sell equipment using Energy Credits. However, it is possible to encounter listings demanding over 1 billion credits for individual items, including equipment whose practical usefulness appears difficult to reconcile with the asking price.

It's a problem familiar to players of many online multiplayer games: speculative pricing and excessive mark-ups can make an otherwise useful marketplace frustrating and inaccessible.

Not everyone has hundreds of millions of credits available or wants to spend countless hours grinding simply to upgrade their ship. An in-game economy should enhance the experience, not become an obstacle to enjoying it.

The relationship between the Exchange and the game's monetisation system also deserves scrutiny.

Players can purchase Zen with real money, obtain tradable items such as Master Keys and sell them for Energy Credits. This creates a route through which real-world spending can help players afford expensive Exchange items.

While there is no evidence presented here that the developers deliberately encourage inflated prices, I believe this economic design raises legitimate questions about whether sufficient safeguards exist to protect ordinary players.

Cryptic Studios, the developer behind Star Trek Online, also developed Neverwinter and Champions Online, both of which feature player trading and premium monetisation. Neverwinter players have similarly raised concerns about expensive Auction House listings and the cost of equipment progression.

This is therefore not an unfamiliar challenge for a developer with extensive experience operating online games and their economies.

Other developers have introduced measures to address marketplace problems. EVE Online's developer, CCP Games, acknowledged concerns about speculation and artificial scarcity within its PLEX market in 2025, while RuneScape has implemented transaction taxes and other economic safeguards.

If other developers can take steps to improve their player-driven economies, surely it is reasonable to expect Cryptic Studios to examine whether similar improvements would benefit Star Trek Online.

There is also considerable irony in a Star Trek game, based on a future where humanity has supposedly moved beyond greed and the relentless pursuit of wealth, featuring a marketplace where some asking prices seem completely disconnected from the needs of ordinary players.

It feels less like Starfleet and more like the Ferengi Alliance!

Ultimately, Star Trek Online remains a good game with enjoyable combat, excellent ship variety and plenty of content. However, the Exchange's excessive asking prices and the difficulties casual players can face when trying to improve their equipment seriously detract from the experience.

I believe the developers should take greater responsibility for ensuring that the marketplace remains accessible and balanced, with better pricing transparency, sensible economic safeguards and more opportunities to obtain competitive equipment through normal gameplay.

Star Trek Online should be about exploration, adventure and commanding starships, not struggling to navigate a marketplace where desirable equipment can carry astronomical price tags.

Final Verdict: 3/5 Stars

A great Star Trek experience spoiled by an excessively expensive player marketplace and legitimate concerns about how its economy interacts with real-money monetisation. The game deserves better, and so do its players.

review_text: I'll have to be honest about this. The game itself is fun to play, but Egosoft needs their knuckles rapped for the pathetic story line (if you can even call it that).  One should expect to see continuity between XBTF and X:Tension, but X:tension simply doesn't provide it.  Hey, remember me? I'm  Kyle Brennan, the Hero of Argon and loved by all of the races for my part in the Xenon War. So then why does no one even know me now, plus the Split and Piranad are downright hostile? I was in a sector called Brennan's Triumph, and the Split told me to sod off. What happened to my trading empire and my million plus credits I usually carried with me?  Egosoft no doubt spent quite a bit of money developing that video with the kid telling us about Captain Brennan. Unfortunately, the video does nothing to explain what happened to Brennan's mines and fabs, or why the prices of almost everything have skyrocketed. Would it have been so hard to find a reason?  Of course not. I took a few minutes and came up with this:   After the Xenon's mother ship was destroyed, Ban Danna gave Brennan those fantastic 125mw shields, which he promptly used to wipe out the Xenon ships and bases in all of their sectors. In retaliation, the Xenon staged a major attack that destroyed all of Brennan's possessions and caused prices to skyrocket among all of the races. The Xenon also put a large bounty on Brennan's life, causing Ban Danna to advise him to go incognito for a while. Danna gave him an Argon buster and a few thousand credits to start out on his own. (Brennan couldn't draw on his own account, since that would reveal where he was.)  And then the game could proceed as it does, but at least there would be a reason for Brennan's sudden poverty and unpopularity. Surely their professional writers could have done even better. Having said that, I do like the way the game is put together and recommend it for many hours of fun.  Still, Egosoft really dropped the ball when it came to setting the stage for Brennan's new adventures.
